lead.t:
May be idiopathic
Commonly diagnosed in non-smoking women in their 5th decade
Often associated with connective tissue disorders, Hypersensitivity Pneumonitis and HIV.
5-year survival rate is 80%.

b: An immunologically mediated inflammatory lung disease primarily affecting the alveoli, also known as allergic alveolitis .
Usually occupational, triggered by heightened sensitivity to inhaled antigens such as moldy hay, contaminated water, bird feathers, or isocyanates.
Unlike asthma (which affects the bronchi), damage occurs at the alveolar level , manifesting as restrictive lung disease with decreased diffusion capacity, compliance, and total lung volume.
Bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) reveals increased CD4+ and CD8+ T lymphocytes.

Hypersensitivity pneumonitis: immune reaction to organic dusts (see also the ILD note).
A history of bird or mould exposure would raise hypersensitivity pneumonitis, which should be excluded.

ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis is an immune‑mediated lung injury that starts in the alveoli after inhalation of organic antigens. It presents as a restrictive pattern with impaired diffusion and can progress to fibrosis if exposure continues.

sections.p: An immunologic reaction to inhaled organic antigens that injures alveolar walls, leading to inflammation and, if persistent, fibrosis. Diagnosis combines exposure history, clinical features, imaging, and BAL lymphocytosis.
b: Exposure to moldy hay, bird feathers, or industrial dusts

t.b: Shows ground‑glass opacities and centrilobular nodules; persistent findings suggest chronic disease.
Elevated CD4+ and CD8+ cells; a lymphocyte percentage >20% supports the diagnosis.
Positive to specific antigens confirms sensitization but is not mandatory.

sections.p: Staging follows the 2015 ATS/ERS guidelines: acute, subacute, chronic. Chronic disease is further graded by extent of fibrosis on imaging and pulmonary function tests.
b: Acute: flu‑like symptoms, reversible with removal of exposure.
Chronic: progressive dyspnea, restrictive pattern, reduced DLCO.

sections.p: Organic inhalants are the main culprits; occupational exposures are common. In low‑resource settings, environmental molds and bird droppings are frequent.
b: Bird feathers or droppings (bird fancier’s lung)

sections.p: Patients develop a flu‑like illness 4–8 hours after exposure, progressing to cough, dyspnea, and restrictive spirometry. Chronic cases show weight loss and clubbing.
b: Chronic: progressive shortness of breath, dry cough, weight loss

sections.p: A stepwise approach uses history, imaging, BAL, and serology. When tests are unavailable, clinical judgment and empirical exposure avoidance guide management.

t.b: Negative result does not rule out HP.

sections.p: Rapid progression to respiratory failure, severe hypoxemia, or pulmonary hypertension warrants urgent care. Fibrosis can become irreversible.
Eliminate exposure, use corticosteroids for acute flare, and consider immunosuppressants for refractory chronic disease. Supportive care includes oxygen and pulmonary rehab.
b: Azathioprine or mycophenolate for chronic cases

t.b: Avoid long‑term use if infection risk is high.

sections.p: Regular spirometry and imaging track progression. Patient education on avoiding known antigens is essential, especially in rural or occupational settings.
b: Education on safe handling of birds or hay

sections.p: Asthma, sarcoidosis, and interstitial lung disease from other causes can mimic HP. Key differences are alveolar involvement and exposure history.
BAL lymphocytosis may be normal in early disease; chest X‑ray can be unremarkable. A negative antibody test does not exclude HP.
b: Early disease may show normal imaging
Serology can be negative despite exposure

faq.a: If exposure stops early, inflammation can resolve; chronic fibrosis is usually irreversible.

faq.q: Do all birds cause the disease?
faq.a: Only certain species (e.g., pigeons, chickens) produce the antigens that trigger the reaction.
Smoking does not cause HP but can worsen lung function and mask symptoms.

exam: Explain why BAL lymphocytosis supports a diagnosis of hypersensitivity pneumonitis.
Describe the key differences in imaging between acute and chronic hypersensitivity pneumonitis.
Outline the first‑line treatment for a patient with acute hypersensitivity pneumonitis who cannot be exposed to the antigen.
